newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - More at stake at CANTV than just rate delays.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - More at stake at CANTV than just rate delays.

text.p: The honeymoon for Venezuelan telephone company CANTV, currently the country's most closely watched stock, is over.

And as worried investment notes skid across fund managers' desks downgrading CANTV from buy to hold, and from hold to sell, with the company's fading bloom so too has wilted international investors' romance with Venezuela, analysts said.

CANTV stock has slid 15 percent since Transport and Communications Minister Moises Orozco last week ruled out a second quarter 4.18 percent tariff increase, due under the 1991 concession agreement, until CANTV justified its costs structure.

"In saying the cost structure of the company will have to be discussed, Orozco implied that pricing in future may be used to limit the profitability of CANTV," investment house ABN-AMRO said in a recent research note.
Orozco said that under the terms of the original contract, either party can seek changes in the tariff setting mechanism in the third, sixth, and eighth years.

"Confidence in the wider market has been shattered," said Alex Dalmady, an analyst at local research firm InvestAnalysis. He noted that while the Caracas bolsa is down over seven percent in real terms this year, Latin America's other markets have surged upwards of 12 percent.
Rumbling labor troubles among CANTV's workforce -- set to strike indefinitely Thursday over a 154 percent pay rise claim -- is indicative of wider social problems unnerving investors.
"This is not an arbitrary caprice, nor an imposition, but a right to review the tariff schedule, that's what we are asking CANTV," Orozco said Tuesday.
CANTV tariffs rise with lagged increases in the wholesale price index, a system that gives rising profits in years of falling inflation, but falling profits as prices rise.
But more is at stake than company profitability, analysts say.

Persistent rumors of President Rafael Caldera's failing health further compound investors' concern as Venezuela embarks on a ambitious year that will require solid political support: $2 billion iron and aluminum privatization, overhaul of the social security system, opening of the mining and electricity sectors, and judicial reform.
"Our main worries are related to the political situation in Venezuela and the possibility that support for the...reform process is slipping," said ABN-AMRO.
As far as CANTV is concerned, analysts believe the company can weather the strike, should it happen.
"Service may be bad for a while, which should backfire against the unions. But the strike's not that important for the stock," said Banco Santander analyst Jose Corral.

Company officials are also sanguine. Two thirds of the company's 17,300 strong workforce is non-unionized, and automated back-up systems require minimal manning so "most people won't be affected (by the strike)... although there may be some sabotage," said a CANTV source who asked to remain anonymous.
The IMF's continued monitoring of the economy also suggests the rate hike's delay is not a final decision.

"Too much is at stake, the company has too high an international profile ... we think the tariffs will be raised, although not in April as scheduled," said Santander's Corral, who believes the company is still attractively priced.
Many Venezuelans also have a stake in the company, 83,000 buying 73 million shares in the one billion dollar November share offering under schemes designed to spread popular capitalism.

CANTV's case is outwardly similar to utility Electricidad de Caracas, a company in near constant battle with the populist-minded Minister of Energy and Mines, Erwin Arrieta, over delayed rate increases.
Analysts note that Orozco -- generally considered an honest and competent minister -- was previously defense minister and general to boot, is used to strong arm tactics.
"We're not worried that rate delay represents a wider change in economic policy," InvestAnalysis' Dalmady said.
"More worrying is that no-one has tapped Orozco on the shoulder and said Hey, you can't do this, don't be so macho'. It points towards some poltical weakness higher up," he added.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
